title: OSINT Methodology: Legal Collection, Analyst OPSEC, and Research Personas
intro: Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) is the discipline of collecting, verifying, and analyzing information that anyone can lawfully access, in order to answer a specific question for a decision maker. This lesson teaches the method behind it: the intelligence cycle, the legal and ethical limits, analyst operational security, non-attributable research accounts, source grading, evidence handling, and a complete safe workflow for investigating a suspicious domain without touching the attacker's infrastructure.

sections.heading: What OSINT is and where a SOC uses it
sections.content:
OSINT is intelligence derived from publicly available sources: websites, public registries, certificate logs, code repositories, news, public social posts, archived pages, leaked-data reporting, and similar material. Three words in that definition matter. Publicly available means you do not bypass a login, a paywall you are not entitled to, or any technical access control. Intelligence means the output is analyzed and tied to a question, not a pile of screenshots. For a decision maker means someone will act on it: block a domain, file a takedown, warn an executive, or scope an incident.

A useful comparison is a library research desk. The books are open to everyone, but a good researcher starts with a question, knows which shelves to check, records where each fact came from, and rates how much to trust each book. A bad researcher grabs whatever is nearby and trusts the loudest source.

The SOC uses OSINT in five recurring ways:

| Use case | Question being answered | Typical output |
|---|---|---|
| Threat intelligence | Who is behind this campaign, and what else do they use? | Related domains, infrastructure clusters, TTP notes |
| Phishing and domain investigation | Is this domain malicious, who registered it, when did it appear? | Verdict, IOCs, takedown package |
| Brand and executive protection | Is someone impersonating our brand or exposing our executives? | Lookalike-domain list, fake-profile reports |
| Incident enrichment | What is known publicly about this IP, hash, or sender? | Context added to the case |
| Attack-surface discovery of your OWN organization | What does the internet already see of us that we forgot? | Exposed assets, leaked credentials, stray cloud buckets |

The fifth row is the safest and often the highest value: you are investigating your own footprint, so authorization is straightforward and the findings are directly fixable.

What is important to know: open does not mean harmless. Collecting information about a person creates privacy obligations even when every fact was public. A domain registrant, a social profile, or a developer handle may belong to an innocent bystander whose infrastructure was compromised or whose name was stolen.

What is important to ask: what decision does this support, what is the minimum I need to collect to support it, and who will be affected by what I write down? Tools for WHOIS, passive DNS, and internet-wide scanners are covered in the enrichment-tools lesson and the threat-intelligence lesson. This lesson is about the method and discipline that surrounds those tools.

sections.heading: The intelligence cycle applied to OSINT
sections.content:
Professional intelligence work follows a repeating loop, described in military and national doctrine and adopted by corporate threat intelligence teams. Following it is what separates an investigation from random browsing, and it protects you from the most common failure: collecting endlessly without a goal.

| Phase | What happens | OSINT example | Common failure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direction (planning) | A requirement is set: question, scope, deadline, audience | Is the reported domain part of a campaign against our customers? Report due in 4 hours | No written question, so the work never ends |
| Collection | Gathering raw data from chosen sources | Registration records, certificate transparency entries, archived pages | Collecting what is easy instead of what answers the question |
| Processing | Normalizing and organizing raw data | Defang URLs, deduplicate, convert timestamps to UTC, translate text | Mixed time zones, lost source links |
| Analysis | Turning data into judgments with stated confidence | These three domains share a registrant pattern and hosting, likely one actor | Treating correlation as proof |
| Dissemination | Delivering to the right audience in a usable form | IOC list to the SOC, takedown request to legal, summary to management | One report format for every reader |

A fifth, ongoing element is feedback: the consumer says whether the product helped, and the next requirement is refined.

Direction deserves the most care. A good requirement is specific and answerable, for example: Determine whether the domain in ticket 4412 is operated by the same actor as the three domains we blocked last month, using only passive public sources, and report by 15:00. Notice it contains a question, a boundary on method, and a deadline. A bad requirement is: look into this domain.

What is important to know: collection should be driven by the requirement and by a source plan, not by the tool that happens to be open. Analysts who start collecting before writing the question usually over-collect, which increases both legal exposure and noise.

What is important to ask: What is the exact question? What would change my conclusion? When is this good enough? Who reads the result and what will they do with it?

Processing is underrated. Timestamps from different sources arrive in different zones and formats. Defanging indicators (writing hxxp and [.] instead of live links) prevents accidental clicks by you or by a colleague opening your notes. Preserve the original source link next to every extracted fact, because analysis later depends on knowing where each fact came from.

sections.heading: Legality and ethics: what you may collect and how
sections.content:
The most important rule of OSINT is that your methods must be lawful and authorized, whatever the target did. A phishing operator committing fraud does not give an analyst permission to commit a crime in return. This section is general education, not legal advice: laws differ by country, and your organization's legal or privacy team owns the final answer.

Four boundaries apply in almost every jurisdiction.

First, do not access non-public data. Logging into a service with guessed, shared, stolen, or leaked credentials; using an exposed admin panel; downloading from an open storage bucket that clearly holds private data you were not meant to see; or bypassing a paywall or rate limit with tricks can violate computer misuse and unauthorized access laws such as the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act or the UK Computer Misuse Act, or their local equivalents. If you stumble onto exposed private data, stop, record only what is needed to report it, and escalate. Do not browse it.

Second, respect terms of service. Many platforms forbid automated scraping, fake accounts, or use of data for profiling. A ToS breach may not be a crime, but it can get your organization's accounts banned, expose it to civil claims, and make your evidence look sloppy.

Third, respect privacy law. Collecting and storing personal data about individuals (names, photos, addresses, employment history) can fall under data-protection regimes such as GDPR even if the data was public. Practical consequences: have a stated purpose, collect the minimum, protect what you store, and delete it when the case closes unless retention is justified.

Fourth, scope and authorization. Work under a written ticket or requirement. Investigating a colleague, an ex-partner, a journalist, or a competitor because you are curious is misuse of access and is often a firing offense.

Ethical limits go further than the law:

- No entrapment: do not lure a person or an actor into committing a crime they would not otherwise commit.
- No harassment or doxxing: do not contact, shame, or publish personal details of a suspect. Findings go to the case owner, legal, or law enforcement.
- No impersonation of real people.
- Proportionality: the harm of collecting must be justified by the risk you are addressing.

The key distinction is passive observation versus interaction. Reading a public page or a public record is observation. Sending a message, joining a private group, filling a form, clicking a tracking link, or making your system connect to the target's server is interaction, and it can alert the target, change the evidence, or cross legal lines. Default to passive. Move to anything more only with explicit approval from legal and your manager.

What is important to ask: Is this source public to everyone? Does it need me to deceive anyone? Would I be comfortable explaining this step to a court, a regulator, and the person being investigated?

sections.heading: Analyst OPSEC: why you never investigate as yourself
sections.content:
Operational security (OPSEC) for an investigator means preventing two bad outcomes: the target learns they are being watched, and the target learns who you are. Both can ruin the investigation and put people at risk.

Consider what happens when you open a suspicious site from your normal work laptop. The attacker's server logs your source IP address, which belongs to your company's known egress range. Your browser sends a user-agent string, language, screen size, and sometimes a referrer. Many phishing kits and malicious sites check visitors against lists of security vendors and corporate ranges, then serve a harmless decoy to defenders and the real payload to victims. Worse, some operators watch their logs for repeated visits from a specific brand, which tells them the takedown is coming and prompts them to move.

The attribution leaks that catch analysts most often:

- Browsing from a corporate IP range or the corporate network proxy.
- Being logged into a personal or corporate account in the same browser profile, so cookies and single sign-on link your identity to the visit.
- Using a real name or a work email on any research account.
- Viewing a professional-network profile while logged in, which can show the profile owner a notification that your company looked at them.
- Browser extensions, saved passwords, and autofill that expose identity details.
- Mixing investigations: opening two unrelated cases in the same browser, which cross-links them through shared cookies.

Build a layered research environment:

| Control | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Dedicated research machine or virtual machine, restored from a clean snapshot per case | No personal data, no history carried between cases |
| Separate browser profile with no sign-ins, extensions limited to what the work needs | Prevents account and cookie linkage |
| Commercial VPN or dedicated research egress, approved by your organization | Source IP is not your corporate range |
| Compartmentalization: one case, one profile, one set of notes | A leak in one case does not expose the others |
| Isolated network segment with no route to internal systems | If something is malicious, it cannot reach your network |
| Device and time-zone hygiene | Avoid leaking local language or time zone through the browser |

What is important to know: a VPN is not magic. It hides the source IP from the target but moves trust to the VPN provider, and it does nothing about browser fingerprinting or logged-in accounts. Treat the VPN as one layer.

A second key point: strong OPSEC for passive work usually means not visiting the target at all. The best way to avoid a footprint on the attacker's server is to use sources that never connect to it, such as archived copies, certificate logs, and registration records.

What is important to ask: What will the target see of me if I do this? Is this machine and profile clean for this case? Does my organization approve this tooling and network egress?

sections.heading: Research accounts and personas: a defensive concept with hard limits
sections.content:
A research account, often called a sock puppet, is an account created by an investigator under a fictional or non-identifying profile so that investigative viewing is not tied to the analyst or the employer. The purpose is OPSEC, not deception of a real person. If a threat actor monitors who views their public profile or channel, a viewing account named after your security team announces your interest, while an anonymous viewing account reveals nothing.

Why teams use them. Some public content is only visible to signed-in users. Some services show the profile owner a list of viewers. Some investigators need to follow the public posts of a known fraud channel over weeks without exposing the investigating company.

What a defensible research persona is:

- A generic, clearly fictional profile that does not claim to be a real, identifiable person.
- Created and registered through an approved process, with the account inventory and purpose recorded internally.
- Used from the isolated research environment and egress described earlier, never from corporate or personal devices.
- Kept for passive viewing only: reading public posts, viewing public profiles.

What it must never be:

- An impersonation of a real person, a real employee, a real brand, or a real victim. Using someone's actual photo or identity is both unethical and often illegal.
- A tool for befriending, messaging, or joining private groups to extract information. That is interaction, and it moves into social engineering and potential entrapment.
- A way to evade a platform ban placed on your organization.
- A source of sensitive data collection about private individuals.

Platform rules matter. Many services require that accounts represent real identities or ban fake accounts outright, and some provide explicit research or law-enforcement channels. A persona that violates the platform's terms can be closed, can taint your evidence, and can create legal exposure for your employer. Before using one, get legal sign-off and check the current rules of the platform in question.

Persona hygiene pitfalls:

- Reusing a phone number, recovery email, or profile photo across personas, which links them together.
- Logging in from the wrong browser profile once, which permanently ties the persona to your real network history.
- Letting the persona accumulate activity that looks automated or suspicious, which triggers verification and bans.
- Forgetting to retire the persona when the case ends.

What is important to ask: Can this be done without logging in at all? Is a persona approved for this case? Am I only reading, or am I about to interact? If the answer to the last question is interact, stop and escalate.

sections.heading: Source reliability, verification, and bias
sections.content:
A fact is only as useful as your confidence in it. Intelligence services solved this with a two-part rating that separates how trustworthy the source is from how credible the specific information is. The scheme, often called the Admiralty system or NATO source and information evaluation, uses a letter for the source and a number for the information.

| Source rating | Meaning | Information rating | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Completely reliable, proven track record | 1 | Confirmed by other independent sources |
| B | Usually reliable | 2 | Probably true, consistent with other information |
| C | Fairly reliable | 3 | Possibly true, not confirmed |
| D | Not usually reliable | 4 | Doubtfully true |
| E | Unreliable | 5 | Improbable |
| F | Reliability cannot be judged | 6 | Truth cannot be judged |

The two ratings are independent. A trusted registry (A) can hold a stale record, so the information may be 3. An anonymous forum post (F) can contain a claim that is later confirmed by two other sources, so it becomes F1. A rating such as B2 is a compact way to tell the reader how much weight to give a statement.

Verification techniques:

- Corroborate with independent sources. Two articles that both copied the same press release are one source, not two. Two tools that both query the same underlying data feed are one source.
- Check provenance. Where did the information originate, and who benefits if you believe it?
- Check the time. Old data presented as current is the most common error. A registration date, a screenshot, or a cached page needs its capture date.
- Verify media. Reverse image search can reveal that a profile photo is stolen. Metadata can be stripped or faked, so treat it as a lead, not proof.
- Treat attribution carefully. Shared hosting, shared registrars, and reused templates are weak signals, because many unrelated actors use the same providers.

Cognitive bias is the largest threat to analysis, more than any technical limitation:

- Confirmation bias: noticing only evidence that supports the first theory. Counter it by actively listing what would disprove your hypothesis.
- Anchoring: letting the first data point dominate. Counter with at least two competing hypotheses.
- Availability bias: assuming the actor you read about last week is behind everything.
- Mirror imaging: assuming the attacker thinks and behaves as you would.

Write conclusions with calibrated language, such as assessed with moderate confidence, and separate facts (the certificate was issued on this date) from judgments (the domain was likely prepared for a campaign). Stating confidence is not weakness. It is what allows the reader to make a good decision.

What is important to ask: How do I know this? Is this one source or many? What would prove me wrong?

sections.heading: Recording and reporting: notes, hashes, and chain of custody
sections.content:
OSINT findings are often used for takedown requests, legal action, insurance claims, or handover to law enforcement. If your evidence cannot be shown to be authentic and unaltered, it may be worthless. Good recording habits cost minutes and protect weeks of work.

Contemporaneous notes. Write notes while you work, not afterward from memory. Record the case number, the requirement, your name, the date and time in UTC, the research machine used, the egress IP, the source visited, the query or search terms, and what you saw. If you later changed course, note why. A timestamped, sequential log shows your method and lets another analyst reproduce it.

Capturing evidence:

- Take full-page screenshots that include the address bar, the date and time, and the visible content. A cropped image without a URL is almost useless.
- Save the source in a durable form: saved page, PDF print, or raw record, not only a screenshot.
- Capture the context around a claim, because a single post without its thread can be misleading.
- Preserve exact URLs and identifiers, and write them defanged in documents and live in a controlled evidence record.

Hashing and archiving. After capture, compute a cryptographic hash (SHA-256) of each evidence file and store the hash in your notes. If the file is later modified, even by one byte, the hash changes, which demonstrates integrity. Keep originals in a read-only evidence location and work from copies. Public web archive services can also store a dated snapshot of a page, but note the caveat: asking an archive service to fetch a live page makes that service connect to the target, so use it only when that interaction is approved, and prefer checking whether an existing snapshot already exists.

Chain-of-custody awareness. Chain of custody is the documented history of who held the evidence, when, where, and what was done with it. Even for OSINT, record who captured it, where it is stored, who accessed it, and any transfers. Standards such as ISO/IEC 27037 and NIST SP 800-86 describe this thinking for digital evidence. Your legal team will tell you the exact standard needed for a given case.

Handling and sharing. Mark reports with a sharing label, for example the Traffic Light Protocol (TLP): CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER, or RED, which tells recipients how widely they may redistribute. Remove personal data that the reader does not need. Keep sensitive evidence encrypted and access-controlled, and delete it per the retention policy.

Report structure that works: a one-paragraph bottom line, the requirement answered, key findings with source ratings, indicators in defanged form, confidence statement, gaps and what was not checked, and recommended actions.

What is important to ask: Could a colleague reproduce this from my notes? Can I prove this file is unchanged? Who is allowed to see this report?

sections.heading: Worked example: planning a passive investigation of a reported phishing domain
sections.content:
Scenario. A customer forwards a phishing email. The link points to a domain that imitates your company login page, written here in defanged form as hxxps://secure-c0rp-login[.]example. You are asked to determine whether it is malicious, whether it belongs to a wider campaign, and what to do about it, without interacting with the attacker.

Step 1: Direction and scope. Write the requirement: assess whether the reported domain impersonates our brand, identify related infrastructure, and recommend blocking and takedown actions, using only passive sources, within four hours. Confirm that the ticket authorizes this work. State what is out of scope: visiting the site from any corporate system, submitting data to the page, contacting the registrant, or accessing anything behind a login.

Step 2: OPSEC setup. Open a clean research virtual machine from a snapshot, on an isolated network segment, with approved research egress. Use a fresh browser profile with no sign-ins. Start a notes file with case number, UTC time, machine, egress IP, and requirement. Defang the indicator in all notes.

Step 3: Extract everything from the report itself. The email headers, sender domain, links, and any attachments are your first-party evidence. Preserve the original message with its headers, hash it, and record who forwarded it and when. This already tells you a great deal without touching the target.

Step 4: Passive source plan. Choose sources that do not connect to the suspect server:

| Question | Passive source type |
|---|---|
| When was the domain registered, by whom, through which registrar? | Registration data lookup (RDAP or WHOIS) and historical records |
| What certificates were issued and when? | Certificate transparency logs |
| What IPs has it resolved to, and what else shared them? | Passive DNS data |
| Has it been reported already? | Public blocklists and reputation feeds |
| Does it look like a brand lookalike? | Your own lookalike-domain monitoring, similarity comparison with your brand |
| What did the page look like? | Existing archived snapshots, if any |

Details of these tools are in the enrichment-tools lesson. A note on a common trap: public URL scanning services fetch the page on your behalf. That is interaction by proxy, since the target still sees a visit from the scanner. It may be acceptable if approved, using the private scan option, but it is not the same as purely passive collection, and public scan results can themselves be seen by others, including the attacker.

Step 5: Analysis. Ask what hypotheses fit. A domain registered days ago, with a certificate issued the same day, imitating your brand with a character substitution, hosted on infrastructure shared with other lookalikes, strongly supports phishing. Before concluding, test the alternative: could it be a legitimate brand-protection domain, a partner, or a parked domain? Rate each fact with source and information grades. Avoid naming a person or a group as the actor based on hosting overlap alone.

Step 6: Document and hash. Capture screenshots of each source result with timestamps, save raw records, compute SHA-256 hashes, and store them in the case folder with a custody note.

Step 7: Disseminate. Send IOCs to the SOC for blocking, a takedown package to the registrar and hosting provider through legal or brand protection, and a short assessment with confidence level to management. Label with TLP. Do not contact the registrant, whose name may belong to an innocent person whose details were abused.

Step 8: Close. Revert the VM, retire any temporary accounts, and apply the retention policy. Record what you did not check, such as active content analysis, so that a separate approved sandbox process can pick it up if needed.

quiz.question: A phishing report contains a link to a lookalike domain. You want to see the login page. What is the best way to proceed within OSINT discipline?

options.label: Open the link from your work laptop quickly, since a single visit cannot do any real harm
Collect from passive sources first, and view the live page only if approved, from an isolated research VM with approved egress
Enter a fake username and password to see how the phishing kit responds and where it sends the data
Ask a colleague to open the link from their home computer so the visit is not tied to the company

quiz.explanation: Passive sources (registration data, certificate logs, passive DNS, existing archives) answer most questions without any connection to the attacker, and a live visit is an interaction that needs approval and an isolated, non-attributable environment. Opening it from a work laptop exposes the corporate IP and risks infection or a decoy page for defenders. Submitting credentials is interaction with attacker infrastructure and can cross legal and ethical lines. Using a colleague's personal computer moves the risk to an unmanaged device and an uninvolved person, and it still is not a controlled, documented process.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly describes the source and information rating (for example B2) used in the Admiralty or NATO scheme?

options.label: The letter grades how credible the specific claim is, and the number grades how reliable the source has been
Both parts measure the same thing, so a high letter always implies a high number for the same item
The letter grades the reliability of the source and the number grades how credible the specific information is, as separate judgments
The rating measures how severe a threat is, from A and 1 as most severe down to F and 6 as least

quiz.explanation: The scheme deliberately separates two questions: how reliable is the source in general (letter), and how credible is this particular piece of information, especially after corroboration (number). A trusted source can still pass along a doubtful claim, and a weak source can supply a claim later confirmed elsewhere. Reversing the meanings misreads the scale. Treating the parts as one measure removes the point of the system, and the scheme grades confidence in information, not the severity of a threat.

quiz.question: An analyst wants to follow the public posts of a fraud group over several weeks. Which approach fits an ethical, defensible use of a research persona?

options.label: Use an approved, clearly fictional account from the isolated research environment strictly to read public content, with legal sign-off
Create a profile using the photo and name of a real employee at the fraud group's target to look believable
Send friendly messages to the group's members and ask to join their private channel so more information can be collected
Log in with the analyst's personal account because it already has a real history and is less likely to be banned

quiz.explanation: A research persona is an OPSEC measure: a non-identifying viewing account, approved and recorded, used only for passive reading and kept away from corporate or personal identity. Using a real person's photo and name is impersonation. Messaging members and asking to join private channels is interaction, which moves into social engineering and possible entrapment. Using a personal account ties the investigation to the analyst's real identity and exposes them to the group and to the platform's rules.

quiz.question: You captured a screenshot of a suspect page and a saved copy of the raw record for a takedown request. What should you do next to preserve the evidence's value?

options.label: Edit the screenshot to highlight the key area and overwrite the original so only one file exists
Keep the files in your downloads folder and describe them from memory when the legal team asks
Send the files by chat to the team and delete your local copies to avoid storing personal data
Compute a SHA-256 hash for each file, store originals read-only, and log who captured them, when, and where they are kept

quiz.explanation: A recorded hash shows the file has not changed since capture, a read-only original supports integrity, and the custody log documents who held the evidence and when. Overwriting the original with an edited version destroys the authentic record, so annotate a copy instead. Relying on memory and an unmanaged folder leaves no proof of integrity or timing. Sending files through chat and deleting your copies loses control of where evidence lives and who has access, which breaks custody.

quiz.question: Two sources both say a domain belongs to the same actor as a past campaign. You notice that one article simply repeats the other's wording. How should this affect your analysis?

options.label: Count them as one source, look for independent corroboration, and state a lower confidence until you find it
Count them as two independent confirmations, because agreement between sources is always strong evidence
Ignore both and reject the hypothesis, since any single repeated claim must be false
Raise the source rating of both to A, because the repeated claim is now widely available

quiz.explanation: Independence is what makes corroboration valuable. A source that copies another adds no new evidence, so treat the pair as one and keep the information rating modest until a truly independent source supports it, while stating your confidence honestly. Counting echoes as confirmation is a classic confirmation-bias error. Rejecting the claim outright is also unjustified, since it may be true but is unverified. Source reliability is judged by track record, not by how often a claim is repeated.
